albums.blurb: Terry Riley is the Californian composer whose 1964 piece In C helped launch musical minimalism. This 1969 Columbia Masterworks LP holds two side-long pieces: the title track layers overdubbed electric organ, electric harpsichord and dumbec percussion into fast interlocking patterns, while "Poppy Nogood and the Phantom Band" sets soprano saxophone against tape-delay loops. Both pieces are entirely instrumental, and Columbia packaged the record for rock audiences rather than the classical bin, which is how it reached a generation of rock and electronic musicians.
albums.reception: Pete Townshend credited the album as the inspiration for the organ part of "Baba O'Riley", whose title is partly a tribute to Riley, and the progressive rock band Curved Air took their name from it.

albums.blurb: The second album by James Mercer's Albuquerque-formed band, released on Sub Pop in October 2003, recorded largely in the basement of Mercer's Portland house and mixed by Phil Ek. Where the debut Oh, Inverted World was hazy and reverb-washed, this one is drier and sharper: ten songs in thirty-four minutes that swing between garage-pop, country-tinged balladry and Mercer's knotty melodic writing.
albums.reception: It holds a Metacritic score of 88, posted what was then the best first-week sales in Sub Pop's history, and was later certified gold by the RIAA.

albums.blurb: Novos Baianos were a communal band from Bahia — singer Baby Consuelo, guitarist Pepeu Gomes and songwriters Moraes Moreira and Paulinho Boca de Cantor — who lived, rehearsed and played football together outside Rio. Their second album grew out of a friendship with João Gilberto, who steered them back toward samba and bossa nova; the record folds those traditions into electric, guitar-driven rock, with the Assis Valente cover "Brasil Pandeiro" and the hit "Preta Pretinha" at its center.
albums.reception: Rolling Stone Brasil ranked it first on its 2007 expert poll of the 100 greatest Brazilian albums of all time.
